opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a great question, and it's something we thought about quite a bit when working on s1. The way I'd frame it: parallel scaling is when you sample many independent answers from the model and then aggregate them, so majority voting, best-of-N with a reward model, that kind of thing. Sequential scaling is when the later computation actually builds on the earlier computation, so the model thinks longer in a single chain, revisits its steps, catches mistakes, and refines its answer.

My intuition, and what we saw in our experiments, is that sequential scaling tends to be more powerful, because each additional token can benefit from everything the model has already worked out. With parallel sampling, every sample starts from scratch. Sample number 64 doesn't know anything about what samples one through 63 tried. So you get diminishing returns pretty quickly, and with majority voting you're fundamentally limited by whether the model gets the right answer reasonably often to begin with. If the correct answer is rare, voting won't surface it.

In s1 we had this simple technique we called budget forcing. If the model tries to stop thinking too early, you suppress the end-of-thinking delimiter and append something like "Wait," which nudges it to keep reasoning and often to double-check itself. You can also cap the thinking at a certain budget. That gave us a pretty clean knob for sequential scaling, and when we compared it against majority voting on the same base model, the sequential approach scaled better per unit of compute.

That said, I don't think it's either-or. Sequential scaling has practical limits too. You hit the context window eventually, and if you force the model to keep going too long it can start looping or second-guessing correct answers. And parallel approaches have a big advantage on latency, because you can run all those samples at the same time, whereas sequential thinking is inherently serial. So in practice I think the most compelling direction is combining them: let the model think deeply in each chain, run several chains in parallel, and then aggregate or even have the model reason over the different attempts. Figuring out the best way to allocate a fixed compute budget between going deeper and going wider is still a pretty open and interesting research question.

r001.rationale: It describes parallel scaling as sampling independent answers and aggregating them through majority voting or best-of-N.

r002.rationale: It describes sequential scaling as continuing a single chain, revisiting steps, catching mistakes, and refining the answer.

r003.rationale: It says sequential scaling tends to be more powerful and scaled better per unit of compute than majority voting.

r004.rationale: It says independent samples start from scratch and voting may fail when correct answers are rare, but does not identify repeating the same mistake across computations.

r005.rationale: It states that each additional token can benefit from what the model has already worked out.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is something we thought about a lot when we were working on s1. The way I think about it is that parallel scaling, things like majority voting or best-of-N, is really a way of sampling the model many times and then somehow aggregating. And the model never gets to see its own previous attempts. Each sample is independent. So you're limited by whatever the model can do in a single shot, and you're just hoping that one of the shots is good and that you can identify it.

Sequential scaling is different because each step can actually build on what came before. The model can look at what it did, notice a mistake, and correct it. That's the whole idea behind budget forcing, where we just append "Wait" and let the model keep going. It reconsiders its reasoning, and that's where a lot of the gains come from. In the paper we actually showed that sequential scaling, at the same amount of compute, tends to outperform parallel scaling, at least for the kinds of reasoning tasks we looked at, like math and competition problems. And you can also combine them. You can do sequential scaling with a few parallel samples and then vote, and that gives you a bit more.

Now, sequential scaling does have limits. The context window is one. At some point the model just can't hold all of that in context, or it starts to drift, and you see the curve flatten out. There's also the issue that if the model goes into a loop and just repeats itself, forcing it to continue doesn't help. So in practice, I think the picture is that sequential scaling has a steeper slope but it saturates, and parallel scaling is more of a fallback where you can keep spending compute even once sequential stops helping. The really interesting question going forward is how to get a model that knows on its own when to think longer versus when it has really exhausted what it can do and should just stop.

r001.rationale: It describes parallel scaling as independent samples whose outputs are aggregated through majority voting or best-of-N.

r002.rationale: It says sequential steps build on prior work and the model can notice and correct mistakes as it continues.

r003.rationale: It says sequential scaling tends to outperform parallel scaling at equal compute and has a steeper slope, while noting it eventually saturates.

r004.rationale: It identifies independent samples as limited to single-shot capability, but does not say they can repeat the same mistake across computations.

r005.rationale: It explicitly identifies building on what came before and reconsidering prior reasoning as advantages of sequential scaling.

astra-6.text:
I think they’re complementary. With sequential test-time scaling, you let the model spend more tokens working through a problem—trying an approach, noticing a mistake, and revising it. With parallel scaling, you generate multiple solutions independently and then use something like majority voting or a verifier to select an answer.

The advantage of parallel scaling is that, if you have enough hardware, you can explore a lot of possibilities without increasing latency as much. But you need a way to identify which solution is good. And if every attempt makes the same mistake, generating more attempts doesn’t necessarily help.

Sequential scaling lets the model build on its previous work, which can be useful for problems that require a longer chain of reasoning. But it’s inherently sequential, so you pay in latency, and a longer response isn’t automatically a better response.

So I’d think about how to allocate a compute budget across both: how long should each attempt be, and how many attempts should you run? That balance will depend on the problem and how reliably you can verify the answer.

r001.rationale: It says parallel scaling generates multiple solutions independently, then uses majority voting or a verifier to select an answer.

r002.rationale: It describes spending more tokens on one problem by trying an approach, noticing mistakes, and revising.

r003.rationale: It calls the approaches complementary and discusses balancing them; it does not expect sequential scaling to scale better.

r004.rationale: It notes that if every independent attempt makes the same mistake, generating more attempts may not help.

r005.rationale: It identifies building on previous work as a benefit of sequential scaling.

sol-6.1.text:
I think they’re complementary. With sequential scaling, you give the model more time to work through a problem within one trajectory. It can explore an approach, recognize that something is wrong, and revise it. With parallel scaling, you generate multiple trajectories independently and then try to select or combine the answers.

The advantage of parallel scaling is that you can run those attempts simultaneously, so you can spend more compute without increasing latency as much. But then selection becomes really important. Generating a correct answer somewhere among a hundred candidates isn’t sufficient if you can’t identify it. For something like code, where you can run tests, that’s a lot easier than for an open-ended question.

Sequential scaling lets later reasoning build on earlier reasoning, but it can also get stuck pursuing an unproductive approach. So I don’t think there’s one that’s universally better. A natural combination is to run several reasonably long reasoning trajectories in parallel, then use whatever verification signal you have to choose between them. The interesting question is how to allocate a fixed compute budget between those two dimensions.

r001.rationale: It describes generating independent trajectories and selecting or combining their answers.

r002.rationale: It says a single trajectory can recognize a problem and revise its approach.

r003.rationale: It calls the methods complementary and says neither is universally better; it does not expect sequential scaling to scale better.

r004.rationale: It notes that a sequential trajectory can get stuck, but does not say independent computations may repeat the same mistake.

r005.rationale: It explicitly says later reasoning in sequential scaling can build on earlier reasoning.
